implementation_notes: On the JVM Scala inherits fork/join twice over: ExecutionContext.global is backed by a ForkJoinPool, and every Future.apply runs on that pool, so fork/join means starting Futures for the two halves and combining them with zip/map or a for-comprehension (the join). Future.traverse/sequence fuses a collection of forks into one join, and parallel collections add a data-parallel surface. Blocking inside a Future is the documented way to starve the global pool (the docs show the thread explosion), so wrap blocking calls in blocking { } or inject a dedicated ExecutionContext. The classic RecursiveTask structure is a JVM-level detail that only interop needs.
pitfalls: ExecutionContext.global is a ForkJoinPool sized to availableProcessors: a few long-blocking futures can starve the whole application (the Scala docs demonstrate thousands of threads being spawned); mark blocking sections or supply a dedicated pool.
Await.result inside a pool thread is a deadlock risk - compose futures instead of blocking on them.
An implicitly imported global ExecutionContext hides the scheduling policy from callers; pass it explicitly where tests or SLAs need control.

variants.name: Parallel collections via the scala-parallel-collections module
variants.implementation_notes: Since 2.13 the parallel collections live in a separate module; .par returns a parallel counterpart of the collection whose map/fold/reduce run through recursive splitting and re-combination on the ForkJoinPool. It is the shortest path for bulk data-parallel work - the framework performs the fork/join and the docs describe the split/apply/combine cycle - while the futures route stays the tool for irregular task trees and mixed async workloads. The combine step must be associative (and safe to run out of order).
variants.code_sketch:
import scala.collection.parallel.CollectionConverters.*
val total = (1 to 1000000).par.map(heavy).sum   // split + fork/join inside
pitfalls: Out-of-order semantics: side effects and non-associative folds become nondeterministic (the docs' reduce(_-_) example) - only associative combines are safe.
The module must be declared since 2.13; plain .par imports fail without it.
Parallel collections and futures share the same ForkJoinPool, so blocking tasks throttle both.
